extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers in mathematical logic and foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic exposition of Russell's paradox: statement, formal derivation in naive set theory, philosophical implications, and technical responses (type theory, Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms, alternatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unrestricted comprehension principle
rubrics_metrics.description: For any predicate φ (with x free) there exists a set y such that ∀x (x ∈ y ⟺ φ(x)). In naive set theory this is the axiom schema of unrestricted comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives the formal schema ∃y ∀x (x∈y ⟺ φ(x)) and shows that substituting φ(x) := (x ∉ x) yields ∃y ∀x (x∈y ⟺ x∉x) and hence a contradiction y∈y ⟺ y∉y. Thus unrestricted comprehension is identified as the source of Russell's paradox and as a principle that must be restricted or abandoned to avoid inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of extensionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets are equal iff they have the same elements: ∀x ∀y (∀z (z∈x ⟺ z∈y) ⇒ x = y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a standard axiom included in the formulation of naive set theory; used to characterise sets by their members and part of the background formalism in which the paradox is stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency requirement (avoid contradiction / principle of explosion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An axiomatic set theory must be free of contradictions because, from a contradiction, any proposition can be proved (principle of explosion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses that contradictions like Russell's paradox are disastrous for foundational systems since they would allow proving arbitrary formulas and undermine truth; this motivates restricting comprehension and developing consistent axiom systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of separation (Zermelo's Aussonderung) / restricted comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace arbitrary comprehension with weaker existence axioms that only form subsets of a given set X using definable properties (separation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zermelo proposed this restriction in 1908 to avoid the paradoxes of naive set theory; separation permits forming {z ∈ X | φ(z)} but not forming a set merely from any predicate over the universe, thereby preventing the Russell set from being constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory (ZFC) constraint on comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: ZFC does not assume that for every property there is a set of all things satisfying it; instead, given any set X, any subset of X definable using first-order logic exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains that the Russell object R cannot be constructed as a subset of any set X in ZFC, so R is not a set in ZFC; this is how ZFC avoids the paradox. It also notes ZFC's development (Zermelo plus Fraenkel and others) and relation to first-order logic and the cumulative hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proper classes (e.g., in von Neumann–Bernays–Gödel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects that would lead to paradox if treated as sets (like the collection of all sets not members of themselves) are treated as proper classes rather than sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some extensions of ZFC such as NBG, Russell-like 'big' collections are classes, not sets, so the paradoxical comprehension does not produce a set. The article notes that R can be viewed as a proper class in such theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type theory approach (Russell's doctrine of types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify the logical language to stratify objects into types so that sets cannot consistently be members of themselves (preventing the formation of the Russell set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Russell's own 1908 solution was type theory, which alters the language/formation rules (rather than the axioms). The article references Principia Mathematica and notes that type-theoretic strategies banish the paradox by disallowing the problematic self-membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of foundation (regularity) — forbid circular/ungrounded sets
rubrics_metrics.description: An axiom (introduced by Zermelo around 1930) that forbids 'circular' and 'ungrounded' sets, thereby eliminating sets that contain themselves and supporting a cumulative hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains that foundation incorporates a motivation of type theory—by forbidding sets that are members of themselves (or other cycles) it helps prevent paradoxical constructions and contributes to the view of sets as layered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative hierarchy / von Neumann universe (V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model sets as elements of a cumulative universe V built up from the empty set by transfinitely iterating the power set operation (layers corresponding to ranks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception provides a way to reason about sets informally without running afoul of Russell's paradox: objects like the Russell construction cannot be sets in V. The article presents the cumulative hierarchy as giving a 'natural' description of the intended universe of sets used in ZFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of impredicativity / concerns about impredicative definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Impredicative definitions (where a definition quantifies over a domain that includes the object being defined) were a worry motivating restrictions such as type-theoretic stratification and debates about higher-order vs first-order formulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article discusses historical concerns (Poincaré, Russell) about impredicativity and mentions that Zermelo and others debated higher-order quantification and impredicativity when formulating axioms to fend off paradoxes such as Skolem's and Russell's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative axiomatic or membership modifications (New Foundations, Scott–Potter, double extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other solutions adjust comprehension or membership (e.g., Quine's New Foundations, Scott–Potter set theory, Double extension set theory) to avoid Russell-like paradoxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists these as alternative strategies closer in spirit to type-theoretic modifications or to altering the comprehension/membership scheme; each provides a different route to a paradox-free theory and is presented as an available technical response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrative/heuristic analogies to detect paradoxical comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Use everyday analogies (barber paradox, library catalogue example, Grelling–Nelson, etc.) to reveal and reason about self-referential paradoxes analogous to Russell's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents the barber and catalogue examples to show the intuitive character of Russell-style contradictions and to help non-logicians see why unrestricted self-reference or unguarded comprehension leads to impossibility.
